whatItFakes: Sales in Salem County, New Jersey and in the state's Urban Enterprise Zones are taxed at the full state rate of 6.625 percent; by state law their sellers collect half that, 3.3125 percent.
why: The starting law keeps one state sales-tax rate per state and a local add-on; a county or zone whose state rate is reduced has no row of its own. The Tax Foundation table folds the reduction into a negative local average, which a local add-on cannot be, so New Jersey now has no local-average row, like the other states without local sales taxes.
replacement: A county and zone sales-tax row read from the state statute, so a seller in Salem County or an Urban Enterprise Zone charges its reduced state rate.

whatItFakes: Opening 30-year mortgage rates after April 2019 are the 10-year Treasury plus the 1990-2019 mean FHFA spread, not a published monthly rate.
why: FHFA's monthly survey ended in 2019; public HMDA is annual and Freddie Mac's survey is excluded (CTO ruling on #3959).
replacement: A government monthly mortgage-rate series, or monthly HMDA origination dates if CFPB publishes them. Resolved Oct 20, 2026 (tripwire audit): the spread was sourced and the marker retired when "Macro: the mortgage spread is sourced" landed; the row had stayed open.

whatItFakes: State and local budgets add no impulse to national output beyond their real average, and neither does the federal budget in a world without the budgets engine. Where the budgets engine runs, the federal budget's change from its base is read each month through macroFiscalMultiplier (Oct 14, OPUS-WORLD).
why: Other states' and towns' budgets are not kept in the world, and one town's own budgets are too small a share of the nation to move it.
replacement: Resolved Oct 16 (owner ruling, no fiscal multiplier): the macro engine carries no budget impulse or multiplier. A public dollar moves output through who is paid and what they spend, read by the budgets, regional and jobs engines; the research ranges stay as a check on the totals.

whatItFakes: When a counted household with an open eviction case is filled in, the case follows the household and its lease takes up the arrears the group had run up at notice, from the notice date. Whether the arrears carry over, are cured by the fill-in, or the case closes is the owner's call.
why: A counted household is not a second simulation: filled in, it must be the same household with the same debt (one model, two tiers). No ruling exists on its arrears.
replacement: The owner's ruling on carry, cure or close for a counted household's arrears on fill-in (docs/coordination/OWNER-DECISIONS.md).

whatItFakes: A seat's new member is the seeded candidate whose lived inflation sits closest to the board's middle, chosen without the president or the Senate.
why: OPUS-GOV's nominateAndConfirm (the president's side picks, the real Senate confirms) is on its branch, not yet on this one.
replacement: registerBoardAppointer with nominateAndConfirm once the offices and appointments modules are on the same branch. Done Oct 15 (board-appointer.ts, registered by openSuccession): a governor is named by the president and confirmed by the Senate; a reserve bank president is chosen and approved by the sitting governors. Open rows it brings: SG-WORLD-board-hawk-side and SG-WORLD-board-career-qualification.

whatItFakes: One named business gets a prime-linked credit line from a town lender for the M1-02 proof; no bank chose to lend.
why: The generated opening has no credit lines; banks and loans are M1-06 (OPUS-WORLD, next on the checklist).
replacement: M1-06 credit: banks that lend from their own books and the borrower's record, with lines indexed to prime. Resolved by Second Session D, October 15, 2026: removed the obsolete stand-in writer and changed macro-proof to buildBenchWorld; credit.ts supplies bank applications and prime-linked facilities from the bank and borrower books.

whatItFakes: Guam, American Samoa, the Northern Marianas and the Virgin Islands start from their own latest published unemployment rate held flat (src/core2/data/regional/territories.json; American Samoa from the 2020 Census, the Marianas from a 2017 survey), with the nation's pay and price level and no industry mix.
why: They are outside the CBSA, CBP, LAUS and BEA tables in the repo; their governments' labor statistics are not yet gathered.
replacement: Each territory's own published labor and price statistics (Guam BLS-funded surveys, USVI Bureau of Economic Research, CNMI and American Samoa statistical offices), or the nearest comparable economy, labeled with its source.

whatItFakes: The opening's job seekers are the jobless working-age adults whose money covers the fewest days, as many as the nation's unemployment rate implies against the generated jobs; the other jobless adults sit outside the modeled labor market.
why: The generated opening employs only part of the town (unsupported workplaces are omitted), so most jobless adults are not really unemployed; the two-level population (OPUS-CORE) will hold the rest as counts.
replacement: The two-level population's labor-force counts by place, age and job (CPS and LAUS), with full people filled in from them.
resolution: openSeekers and openCountedSeekers in src/core2/modules/jobs.ts count the jobs held in each place by age band (the named workers and the counted ones alike) and size each band's seekers from the place's own rate (openingRate, the regional series from LAUS) times the band's ratio in src/core2/data/jobs/age-unemployment.json (CPS Table 3); the neediest jobless adults in the band seek.

whatItFakes: A layoff names the business itself as who decided it.
why: Businesses have no recorded owners or managers until businesses growing (M1-08). Resolved Oct 19, 2026: a layoff is decided by the recorded owner, else by the firm's best-paid full worker still on the staff (managerOf in modules/jobs.ts); only a firm with no one left decides as itself.
replacement: The owner or manager person recorded by M1-08, deciding from their own traits and the books.

whatItFakes: Every state's unemployment insurance pays half the lost weekly pay up to $611 a week for 26 weeks after one waiting week, with a $2,775 base-period minimum (the states' medians).
why: Resolved by OPUS-GOV (2026-10-14): jobs-benefits.ts reads lawInForce directly, no stand-in. Was: each state's own terms are law in force on OPUS-GOV's branch (lawInForce(api, "unemployment-insurance")), not yet on this one.
replacement: registerUnemploymentTerms with the state's terms from lawInForce once the laws module is on the same branch.

whatItFakes: A business with no recorded owner (a public employer, an ownerless landlord) applies for a line whenever its cash is below a few months of payroll; owned businesses' owners decide.
why: Businesses have no recorded owners until businesses growing (M1-08). Resolved Oct 19, 2026: a firm with no recorded owner is run by its best-paid full worker, who weighs the same reasons as an owner; with no full person, its counted people's summed pulls decide (modules/credit.ts).
replacement: Those organizations' own deciders (a board, a public budget) choose whether to borrow.

whatItFakes: The town bank opens holding only its own equity as cash and lends from that; households' and businesses' money is not on deposit with it.
why: Deposits need the core's named accounts (OPUS-CORE's accounts item) so cash can sit in bank accounts without a second book.
replacement: Session B: real household and business savings move to the bank through accounts/postJournal; lending reads cash and liabilities. Limited payment-path withdrawal coverage is tracked separately as SG-WORLD-deposit-wallet-buffer.

whatItFakes: All of a town's rentals belong to one landlord business with no owner; it serves notice by summed pulls of months owed and months late (calibrated to landlords filing at about two months owed), not by an owner's own patience and cash.
why: Landlords as businesses with owners who decide from their own books and patience come with businesses growing (M1-08).
replacement: Rentals owned by the town's own landlords (owners of rental businesses and individual owners), each deciding from their traits, cash and the tenant's history.

whatItFakes: Eviction steps not yet read from official text in force on the opening day (January 20, 2025): of 56 places, 42 have the notice period read, 42 whether a tenant can cure, 38 the hearing period and 41 the stay (all four in 31, marked high); the other values come from secondary summaries, and missing values take the median of the better-sourced places. One undated value per place cannot follow a law that changes after the opening day.
why: Official code sites for 14 places refused the cloud or publish only through Lexis or a JavaScript application (AR, AS, CT, GA, GU, IL, IN, MS, NH, NM, NY, PR, TN, VI); AK, AL, HI, MA, MT, NJ, RI, SD, TX, VT and WV leave a hearing or stay to court rules, set no day count, or were read only in text that took effect later. Reads: data/research/world/eviction-statute-reads-2026.json (Oct 23) and data/research/housing/eviction-steps-2026.json (Oct 12).
replacement: Each place's steps read from the official statute text and cited by section, then M1-laws' landlord-tenant law in force. Oct 23, 2026: 46 steps in 21 places read from the statute text in force on January 20, 2025 (data/research/world/eviction-statute-reads-2026.json, checked against housing.json by scripts/research/housing-check.ts); later laws (Hawaii from February 5, 2026, Texas from January 1, 2026, the District from December 31, 2025) are recorded there as dated laterLaw rows for world-housing-eviction-law-dated-phases. Still open for the 25 places above, which need their codes read through Lexis or the courts' rules (research-housing-statutes-remaining).

whatItFakes: An eviction hearing ends in judgment whenever rent is still owed and notice was given, with no judge's discretion, defenses or counsel.
why: Courts are parked until after early access (owner, Oct 10). Resolved Oct 19 by the owner's Oct 14 ruling, 'Evictions without courts: an eviction completes after the state's notice period from the law in force; the household moves as the housing engine moves leavers. No court scene until courts come' (docs/coordination/OWNER-DECISIONS.md, DECISION-REGISTER.md). The hearing step is a dated step of the statute with no judge or scene, which is what the ruling asks for; the courts port is separate work.
replacement: The courts port: a judge deciding from the record, the tenant's defenses and any right to counsel in the law in force.

whatItFakes: The opening's largest businesses (by staff, up to the state's estimated share of jobs in multi-establishment firms) belong to firms based outside the town; every other is owned by its highest-paid current worker, as owner-operator.
why: The generated opening records no owners; founding by choice (this work order's next piece) gives new businesses their real founders.
replacement: Owners from the opening's history (who founded or bought each business, M1-14), with absentee and corporate owners from business ownership records.

whatItFakes: Completed rentals now admit unassigned households in either tier once income and cash qualify, and consume an actual vacancy. Existing-stock arrivals and departures still lack unit-level assignment.
why: New-unit occupancy and its vacancy changes are recorded; the opening rental stock has no individual unit inventory.
replacement: Record opening rental units and route their arrivals and departures through the same assignment and release rules.

whatItFakes: Counted workers (the wider population) retire, quit, start looking and stop looking by summed pulls (strongestPulls) rather than the shared chooser; they apply to every opening in their place, and an employed counted worker accepts by acceptScore. Counted closures and layoffs also run through this path.
why: The shared chooser needs a full person; filling in everyone who makes a job decision would undo the two-level population.
replacement: Fill-in at the moment a counted person meets an employer (OPUS-CORE's fillInPerson), or an aggregate chooser for counted groups agreed with OPUS-CORE.
resolution: counted workers retire, quit, look around, stay, start looking, stop looking and apply by the same offers and the same chooser as full people (workerOffers, reviewCountedWorkers, reviewCountedEntry and the shared weekly consider in modules/jobs.ts), each record deciding for the household weight it stands for. Their record holds no needs, so strain is the neutral zero; age, savings, traits and tenure are read from it, and a decision's recorded reasons are kept on the change or seeker row. Looking and waiting are weighed again each month by one shared rule (settleEntryChoice) for any full or counted person whose search began as their own choice to look (the opening's jobless and those who started looking): waiting wins ends the seeker row and the claim in both tiers; a search that began with a lost job is ended by being hired. The acceptance of an offer by an employed counted worker stays acceptScore, which full people also use.

whatItFakes: Quitting and looking around while employed are now decided by the shared chooser for full and counted workers alike, and win only on a large pay gap, so a played year has far fewer quits than JOLTS reports; the old summed-pull churn that matched JOLTS quit rates is gone.
why: One rule for both tiers replaced the counted summed pulls; the leave and look terms were retuned for retirement and entry, not yet for quits.
replacement: The leave and look terms (quitScore, jobsLookBaseline, jobsPayGapWeight) calibrated so a played year's quits per worker match JOLTS total private quits by month, measured in drawn places.

whatItFakes: Counted owners who found a business, close one or borrow, and a firm with no recorded owner run by counted people, act by summed pulls (strongestPulls) rather than the shared chooser.
why: The shared chooser decides for one actor; these decisions are made for a whole counted group at once.
replacement: Each counted owner decides through the shared chooser from the counted record, times the household's weight, as counted workers now do.

whatItFakes: The wider population's renters pay rent from their group's money (the place's residents account, kept per group), and the arrears they run up are held per group (households of one kind in one place), not per household: which of the group's households are behind is read from the group's arrears, the ones with the least income first. A removed counted household stays counted without a home (tenure none, its record standing for the one household removed) and is placed, counted homeless and rents again from its record (CTO, Nov 1); its cash is its share of the group of households without a home it joins, shared with any other such household of that group. One that doubles up with a relative in another town leaves the counts through the counted moves engine at its coarse grain: to its state's rest-of-state count when the relative's town is in the same state, to the other state's count otherwise, not to the relative's own town as a full household is relocated; without the moves engine it stays in town (a relative there, a shelter bed or the street).
why: The two-level population pools counted households' cash by place (OPUS-CORE's stopgap), so the group falls behind together; a single counted household's own shortfall is not kept.
replacement: Per-household cash for counted households, with arrears and eviction through the same legal steps; until then the group's arrears and money stand for its households'. Counted moves to a named town (the host's), once the counted moves engine keeps towns beyond the governing one.

whatItFakes: A job that a saved visitor agreement names as its provider's qualification is never ended by a layoff, a quit, a retirement or a move to another job.
why: The core rejects the agreement's next payment once the named job ends ("Visitor qualification no longer resolves its actual product job"), seen in year two of Absecon, New Jersey.
replacement: OPUS-CORE lets a visitor agreement re-resolve its qualification to any current qualified worker at the provider; then this filter goes. Resolved by Claude session on the pool item world-agreements-re-resolve-worker, October 19, 2026: deleted src/core2/pinned-jobs.ts and the jobs engine's filters on it. A saved agreement already follows its product jobs' real life in finance-cash.ts (productJobRelations: an ended job drops out and the supplier's current staff in the product occupations carry it; with none, the agreement ends), so a named job's holder may now be laid off, quit, retire or move.

whatItFakes: An owner still in the wider population (not yet filled in) takes the option whose reasons sum highest instead of choosing through the shared chooser, and their draws go to their place's pooled residents account.
why: Filling in every owner as a full person made a game year about 40% slower (Absecon, New Jersey); owners are filled in when the player meets them.
replacement: The shared chooser for counted people (the same reasons, without a full person), or full owners once a full person costs the core little per day. Resolved by Second Session D, October 15, 2026: the shared chooser reads counted owners through the same initial actor shape without admitting them. Draws and closure proceeds reach the recorded owner household group; full owners keep their own accounts.

whatItFakes: Each owner's purchase year comes from the national move-in distribution by age rank, the loan is a 30-year fixed with the NAR median down payment and no refinancing, and the nation's mortgage shares by age apply in every county.
why: The county move-in and mortgage-status tables were not in the data, and no refinancing step exists.
replacement: FHFA house price index by state and metro for purchase prices, ACS B25038 and B25027 by county, and refinancing waves from the rate history. Oct 23, 2026: ACS 2020-2024 B25038 and B25027 for every state and county are in data/research/world/acs-2024-owner-mortgage-moved-in-by-county.json (Census Bureau; checked by scripts/research/housing-check.ts against the national shares openingMortgages reads in src/core2/housing-mortgages.ts); purchase prices already follow the state FHFA index (homePriceRatio). Reading the county rows, and refinancing from the rate history historicalMortgageRate already holds, is world-housing-mortgages-county-shares.

whatItFakes: Home prices follow FHFA's state house price index through its latest quarter (2026 Q2), and Puerto Rico's from FHFA's developmental index; after the latest quarter, and where FHFA has no index (Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands), they follow consumer prices (CPI-U, which in the data ends in 2025). The seller in a purchase is outside the town.
why: FHFA publishes no index for the four island areas, the simulated future has no house price model yet, and people don't move in or out of town until M1-09.
replacement: A house price step in the economy (the region's incomes, rates and vacancy), territorial price data, and sellers who are the town's own owners (M1-09; world-home-sales-set-the-town-price, world-home-turnover). Oct 23, 2026: Puerto Rico now reads FHFA's developmental all-transactions index (FHFA, 2026 Q2; data/research/world/fhfa-hpi-pr-2026q2.json, checked by scripts/research/housing-check.ts) through homePriceRatio in src/core2/housing-prices.ts; still open for the four island areas and for prices after the last quarter.

whatItFakes: American Samoa has no bank branch in the FDIC Summary of Deposits, so its town bank's deposits are the nation's deposits per resident times the town's people. (Guam, the Northern Marianas, Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands are in the county table with their own FDIC branch deposits, so they no longer use this.)
why: FDIC Summary of Deposits has no rows for American Samoa or the Virgin Islands in the data, and island villages carry no county code.
replacement: American Samoa's bank deposits from its territorial banking regulator or the banks' own reports; checked Oct 19 (claude): the FDIC Summary of Deposits for June 30, 2026 lists 16 branches in Guam, 6 in the Northern Marianas, 260 in Puerto Rico and 20 in the Virgin Islands, all already in data/tables/town-deposits.json, and none in American Samoa.

whatItFakes: A place that no Census county table covers and that is not one of the four island areas (American Samoa, Guam, the Northern Marianas, the Virgin Islands, which now start from their own Census 2020 rows) starts from the nation's owner share and household-weighted county medians.
why: Every other place has a Census county tenure, rent and value table or one of the four island areas' own Census 2020 rows; a place with neither has no table of its own in the data.
replacement: That place's own tenure, rent and value table; if no such place is reachable, delete the fallback and this row.

whatItFakes: Where the ACS withholds a county's median rent or home value (a county with very few households: Kalawao, Hawaii; Edwards, Kenedy, Loving and Culberson, Texas), the state's household-weighted county median stands in, then the nation's.
why: Resolved Oct 19 (gov-standins-housing): a county the ACS withholds takes the household-weighted median of its neighboring counties (Census county adjacency, src/core2/data/housing/county-neighbors.json); the state and nation stand in only if no neighbor publishes. world-property-tax-zero-home-values: a missing value read as zero left every owner in the county without a home. world-property-tax-zero-home-values: a missing value read as zero left every owner in the county without a home, so no property tax was collected.
replacement: The county's own median from the ACS 5-year table when it is published, or the median of its neighboring counties.

whatItFakes: A union local's members are the place's employed at its state's 2025 membership rate (the nation's where BLS has no row), paying dues from the wider population's pooled cash; nobody is recorded as a member.
why: The opening records no memberships.
replacement: Members recorded on people (by industry and state, BLS Union Members tables), each choosing to join or leave from their pay, job and views; dues from their own cash.

whatItFakes: The town bank's smallest personal loan is a common published minimum ($1,000), not the bank's own product terms.
why: Community banks' product terms are not in the data.
replacement: A sourced range of community-bank personal loan minimums (FDIC or call-report product data).

whatItFakes: Every owner pays the state's average effective property tax rate, to the outside account, with no assessment cap.
why: The county's rate in force, its cap and its treasury are OPUS-GOV's law in force (lawInForce(api, "property-tax")), on its branch.
replacement: registerPropertyTax with the county's rate, cap and treasury from the law in force.
resolution: The budgets engine registers the rate, cap and payee from the law in force (registerPropertyTax) in every played world; the state-average fallback is deleted, and a place with no law registered is billed nothing. The state average still sizes the opening's outside living cost.

whatItFakes: Property tax is paid a twelfth each month, as through a mortgage escrow, for every owner.
why: Counties bill once or twice a year on their own dates; the dates come with each county's law.
replacement: Bills on the county's due dates from the law in force, with escrow monthly only for owners with a mortgage.

whatItFakes: A compliance duty costs every bound business twice the manufacturing average pollution-abatement share of its operating costs.
why: No per-industry abatement cost data is loaded yet.
replacement: Census PACE abatement operating costs by industry (NAICS), scaled by the standard the county misses.

whatItFakes: Each household takes a public broadband offer as the subscribing share of one household, not by its own choice.
why: Household subscriptions and switching choices are not modeled per household.
replacement: Each household's subscription and its own choice to switch, from its price and service.

whatItFakes: New houses sell only to full renter households; counted renters and households moving in never buy one, so unsold houses pile up.
why: Counted households' money is pooled by place and arrivals are OPUS-CORE's population engine.
replacement: Counted renter households and arrivals buy new houses through the same choice and mortgage, once fill-in and arrivals land.

whatItFakes: A counted worker who retires draws their place's opening retirees' average income (Social Security and pensions from outside the town), not a benefit from their own earnings record and claim age.
why: Counted people have no earnings records; Social Security claims and benefit formulas are OPUS-CORE's and OPUS-GOV's. Resolved Oct 19, 2026: a counted worker who retires claims at once from their own record through claimRetirementNow (modules/retirement-claims.ts), sized as the opening sizes awards; that path stays under SG-CORE-retirement-claims-in-play until the Social Security program.
replacement: The core's Social Security claim for counted retirees, with GOV's benefit rules in force.

whatItFakes: Unemployment insurance is built (a claim after a layoff or closure, the state's law in force, a weekly benefit to the worker) but each benefit is paid from the town's outside account, not from the state's unemployment fund, and nothing collects the employers' contributions into that fund.
why: Narrowed Oct 17 (claude): the row said a spell of unemployment pays nothing; jobs-benefits.ts pays it from the town's outside account. The state fund and the employer contributions into it need the state treasury on the budgets module (M1-07, OPUS-GOV).
replacement: State unemployment insurance under the law in force, paid through postJournal from the state's fund.
resolution: payClaims in src/core2/jobs-benefits.ts pays each benefit from the state treasury on the budgets module, which the employers' state unemployment tax pays into (employer-taxes); a week the treasury cannot cover is advanced from the town's outside account.

whatItFakes: A business whose owner stops working or dies with no worker or family member to take it on keeps running without a recorded owner.
why: The core closes a business only when it can't pay (closeEmployer); there is no voluntary closure for a solvent business yet.
replacement: A core call to wind down a solvent business (end its jobs, contracts and books; the owner keeps what is left), asked of OPUS-CORE; the owner then chooses between closing and selling. Resolved by Second Session D, October 15, 2026: succeed already records no-successor and calls closeByChoice, which uses the core closeBusinessByChoice writer to settle a solvent business. Retired the stale entry after focused closure and played-year checks.

whatItFakes: A counted employer short of cash on payday records a wage shortfall and never draws its approved credit line, though the line has room.
why: The credit engine draws only against a standing finance contract; counted wages are residents flows paid by transfer, so a correct draw needs a finance-engine entry for flows (OPUS-CORE).
replacement: A finance-engine draw for a residents wage flow (journal-balanced, up to the line's room), called from residents settle() before the shortfall is recorded.
resolution: A counted employer short of cash on payday now draws its approved credit line for what its cash and savings could not pay (api.drawWageFlowCredit, a finance-cash credit transfer whose trigger is the wage flow), and only what the line cannot cover is recorded as a shortfall.

whatItFakes: A relative living out of town (a husk) is never an aide candidate, because the records hold no work for them, and an unknown job is not an empty one.
why: Husks are kept as a name and family ties only; their place's work isn't modeled at the coarse level, so whether they are out of work, and so free to take the post, can't be read.
replacement: Work for out-of-town relatives from their place's coarse population (jobs by age and place), after which those within commuting reach and out of work apply like anyone.

whatItFakes: Payroll withholding for a worker who lives outside the town reads the law of the worker's residence from the starting-law rows (the town's recorded rows where a jurisdiction is shared with the town), so a law enacted in play in a jurisdiction the town does not share is not read; a residence the place lookup cannot resolve gets federal and payroll tax only.
why: Enacted laws are recorded only for the town's own chain; other places' chains are not opened as worlds yet.
replacement: Each place's law chain recorded in the laws module, enacted acts included, read for every worker's residence.

whatItFakes: Income tax a worker owes a government with no treasury in the world (another state, or a county or city the world does not model) is not withheld, so the worker's pay is not reduced by it and no money moves.
why: An outside account takes money only against a resolved due-obligation record, and those governments have no treasury account to pay. Resolved Oct 16 (world-withholding-outside-governments): each such government is an outside government with an account, and the tax is withheld and paid to it against a due record the withholding writes.
replacement: Each such government gets a treasury (or an obligation-backed outside flow) and the withheld tax is paid to it.

whatItFakes: A local flat income tax on a row whose base is wages or AGI is taken on the paycheck's gross pay (no pre-tax contributions or personal exemptions are modeled); a row whose base is taxable income is taken after the state (else federal) standard deduction only.
why: The law rows name the base but carry no exemption or adjustment amounts, and workers' pre-tax deductions are not modeled.
replacement: Personal exemptions and adjustments read from the law rows and the worker's own records.

whatItFakes: A worker who lives outside the town pays no county or city income tax to the town's jurisdictions for working there (the rows' nonresident rate is not applied); local tax is withheld only by the law at the worker's residence.
why: Where a worker works and which local jurisdiction taxes nonresident wages is not resolved per paycheck yet.
replacement: Resolve the workplace's local chain per paycheck and apply each row's nonresident rate to residents of other jurisdictions.

whatItFakes: Employers pay no Social Security or Medicare share on wages paid to counted workers through the residents' merged wage flows; only full workers' paychecks carry the employer share.
why: Counted wages are paid by the residents engine's merged flows, not the work payroll the employer-taxes module hooks, and that engine is OPUS-CORE's.
replacement: A residents wage-flow payment hook (OPUS-CORE) that posts the same employer share from the law rows in force. Built Oct 16: the residents engine tells every module each counted payday (onCountedWages) and the employer-taxes module posts the share, per worker times the workers the flow pays.

whatItFakes: An official whose office sits outside the town (a state or federal office, at its seat of government) draws one applicant living where the office sits, generated from the world's seed and the office (name, age in the business-worker range, traits), and records them as a person only when hired.
why: The owner ruled that such an official hires from where the office sits (Oct 14), but the seat's population isn't modeled, so there is no labor market there to read.
replacement: The seat's coarse population (people by age and work, as the town's counted population is kept), from which the official's applicants come by the same reach and working-age reads.

whatItFakes: A business a counted resident owns pays no tax on its profit: under the law its profit is its owner's income, and only owners who are full people pay it (as estimated payments from their own cash). Businesses owned by another organization pay the corporate rate each quarter.
why: A counted owner has no cash account of their own; their income is a group flow, and the income tax engine withholds only from individual accounts and from the counted wage flows.
replacement: The counted owner group's share of the profit taxed by the income tax law in force where they live, as a flow of the owner group. An owner-run business's quarterly profit is taxed as its owner's income: full owners pay from their own cash, counted owners through their household group, by the withholding rule of the income tax law in force (employer-taxes.ts, passThrough and passThroughCounted). Proved in src/core2/profit-pass-through.test.ts.

whatItFakes: Businesses pay no property tax on their premises; the property-tax engine bills homes only.
why: A business's books record no premises or their value, so there is nothing for the property-tax rate in force to read.
replacement: Business premises recorded with an assessed value (commercial values by place), billed at the property-tax rate in force like homes.

whatItFakes: The record a screen would read for a business's books (cash, sales, costs, wages, profit, taxes paid and owed, its credit line) is built, but no screen shows it: whether a player sees another business's books is the owner's open decision.
why: Owner ruling, Oct 14 (business audit question 5): register the question as an owner decision and build the record the screen would read.
replacement: The owner's ruling on who sees a business's books (its owner, the player as owner, public filings only, or anyone), after which OPUS-PLAY shows this record on the screen that ruling names. docs/coordination/OWNER-DECISIONS.md: 'Starting or buying a business: 1.0, not early access. An owner sees the books.' and 'a business closing shows its books' as a dev-mode item. The view (business-books-view.ts) is the owner's and the developer's.

whatItFakes: Until the town has at least macroTownGrowthMinMonths of recorded income with the same months a year earlier (about 15 months into a game), the national step hears a neutral stand-in for the town's income growth: trend growth plus the inflation anchor.
why: The town's income is recorded only from the opening, so a year-over-year growth needs a year of records first.
replacement: The town's income history before the start (from the opening's pre-start years), so growth is read from the first month. Deleted the invented neutral growth input and its published observation. Until comparable paid-income records exist, the national model omits local feedback. Actual observed growth still enters the same model; missing pre-start income history remains explicitly registered as SG-WORLD-macro-income-history.

whatItFakes: The player's household is evicted like any other when its rent goes unpaid: notice, filing, hearing, judgment and removal under the place's law.
why: Whether the player can lose their home is the owner's call (homelessness package, Oct 14); the package's default is yes.
replacement: The owner's ruling: keep it as is, or give the player's household another path. docs/coordination/OWNER-DECISIONS.md, 'Homelessness is a factor' (Oct 14): 'A person who does not work and does not pay loses their home like anyone else; the player's household too.' Same notice, filing, hearing and judgment as anyone (docs/packages/homelessness.md).

whatItFakes: A place's shelter beds are its state's year-round beds per 10,000 people (HUD 2025 Housing Inventory Count) times its own people, not the beds its Continuum of Care actually lists in or near it.
why: The HIC lists beds by Continuum of Care and provider; joining providers' geocodes to places is not done yet.
replacement: Beds by place from the HIC provider rows (geocode to county and place), with occupancy on the count night. Oct 23, 2026: the 2025 HIC project rows are summed by state and city, with HUD geocodes and count-night occupancy, in data/research/world/hud-hic-2025-beds-by-city.json (HUD, 2025; 2,656 city rows; the state rates shelterBeds reads are checked against it by scripts/research/housing-check.ts). Reading them per place is world-housing-shelter-beds-by-place.

whatItFakes: American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands, which have no HUD Continuum of Care, use the median shelter beds per 10,000 of the three island areas the HIC counts (Guam, Puerto Rico, U.S. Virgin Islands), an estimate with a spread of 2.47 to 10.9.
why: No HUD Housing Inventory Count covers them; the island-area median is the nearest measured stand-in (data/research/stopgaps-oct19/D-economy-world.json).
replacement: Each territory government's own shelter count. Oct 23, 2026: none found. American Samoa's Department of Human and Social Services publishes no shelter count, and the CNMI Homeless Coalition's 2018 Saipan count (22 sheltered people, reported by the Saipan Tribune) could not be reopened from the cloud (connection reset, then 503), so the island-area median stays (research-housing-statutes-remaining).

whatItFakes: A state's foreclosure timeline that was not read from its statute (55 places) is taken from secondary summaries; a place with no published average days to complete (42 places) takes the median of its process (nonjudicial 174, judicial 2007, both 2293 days, computed from the 14 published averages) in place of the national average (ATTOM, 563 days in Q2 2026).
why: Foreclosure statutes and timelines were gathered for 56 places in one pass; places below high confidence still need their statute text read.
replacement: Each place's foreclosure steps read from its statute text and court rules, with its own average days to complete. Oct 23, 2026: ATTOM's national figure and the 14 state averages were reopened (Q2 2025, Q3 2025 and Q2 2026 releases), Texas's steps were read from statute text (now high) and Minnesota's sale notice corrected to six weeks (data/research/world/foreclosure-reads-2026.json, checked by scripts/research/housing-check.ts against foreclosure.json, read by foreclosureSteps in src/core2/housing-foreclosure.ts). Still open: ATTOM publishes per-state averages only for its five longest and five shortest states each quarter, and the other statutes are unread (research-housing-statutes-remaining).

whatItFakes: A job offer's deadline stops the player's clock once as a reminder instead of holding it until the player answers; an unanswered offer lapses as the employer's withdrawal.
why: The play screen has no control yet to answer a job offer; a held deadline would stop the clock for good.
replacement: A held offer-deadline stop once the play screen shows jobOffersFor with accept and decline controls (OPUS-PLAY). Done: the play screen answers offers (POST /api/jobs/answer), so the deadline stop is held and settleOffer releases it.

whatItFakes: Completed rentals match local rent-saving tenants, recovered homeless households, and unassigned households in either tier. Job-location and family-space matching are not modeled.
why: Rent, income and cash are read; dwelling capacity and commute preferences still lack records.
replacement: Read recorded job locations and dwelling capacity to weigh commute and family-space changes with the same decision rule in both tiers.

whatItFakes: Savings and withdrawals are reviewed monthly with a three-month wallet reserve; extraordinary payments and estate settlement do not yet request bank withdrawals directly. Dormant claims remain owed, not deleted.
why: The existing payment paths consume cash directly. A bounded monthly policy allows deposits to fund lending without duplicating cash or claiming all payments are deposit-aware.
replacement: Have payment and estate writers withdraw from the same named deposit claim before declaring a cash shortfall; preserve household claims across family changes.

whatItFakes: The bank holds opening mortgages whose original funding is an unmatched opening liability, not named customer deposits. New savings deposits are actual journal transfers and are accounted for separately.
why: The pre-existing mortgage opening subtracts its initial principal from capital without recording who funded it. Retaining that offset avoids creating capital or cash while adding new deposits.
replacement: Generate the mortgage opening with named depositor or warehouse-funding liabilities and retain those funding records in the bank books.

whatItFakes: No town income-growth observation or local feedback is available before enough comparable paid-income months exist; the national economy continues from its national records.
why: The played world records paid town income only from opening and does not have comparable pre-start income receipts.
replacement: Pre-start town paid-income records produced from the opening economy, so year-over-year feedback can be computed from real records immediately. Done Oct 16 (world-stopgap-macro-missing-record): the national step hears the nation's payroll-income growth over the same twelve months as the estimate of the town's growth (townGrowthEstimatePct on each simulated month), and the town's own paid-income growth takes over by a twelfth of the weight for each comparable month it covers (townGrowthOwnWeight). No month omits local feedback.

whatItFakes: A central bank candidate's place on the left-right scale is read from how much inflation they lived through against the board (more is a hawk, on the Republican side), so the president's party picks the candidates nearest their own side.
why: Presidents of either party have named hawks and doves; no source ties a nominee's lived inflation to a party, so this is an assumed link.
replacement: A nominee's party or stated views as a record on the candidate, read for alignment; or a sourced relation between appointing party and hawkishness.

whatItFakes: How qualified a candidate's career makes them is a small table by career, not read from the candidate's record of work.
why: A seeded candidate has a career label and a lived-inflation figure, and no work history to weigh.
replacement: Qualification read from the candidate's recorded career history, with the table's values calibrated to the careers of past governors.

whatItFakes: A town's police, fire, public works and public health departments and its local government offices are paid by the town's own government (its city or village, else its township), a state office in town by its state and a post office by the nation. The opening's data does not say which unit employs a given department, so the link is assumed.
why: The departments held no cash and no pay link, so their workers were never paid. The Census of Governments lists functions by government but not which unit staffs a town's own departments.
replacement: Each department's employing government read from the Census of Governments employment file by function, so a county health department, a fire district or a state agency's field office pays its own staff.

whatItFakes: A person met in a place other than the player's has the age, job and wage that place's counts show, kept as a fact on the person (identity:work), but no employer organization, payroll or household beyond themselves exists there, so no money moves for them and no engine reads the job yet.
why: Only the player's town has employers with accounts and payroll; paying a visited town's workers means a money design for places the regional economy does not step person by person.
replacement: The regional economy pays other places' workers from the place's counts (a wage flow per place, as the player's town has for its unplaced workers), and an engine that decides about a person (a view, a price, an eligibility) reads their job and wage.

whatItFakes: The share of the BLS weekly-earnings gap between education levels that holds within one role and employer (jobsSchoolingPayShare, 0.4). Positions are already priced for their occupation, which carries part of the schooling premium, so only a share of the raw gap moves a hire's pay.
why: No source measuring the within-occupation, within-employer schooling premium was fetched; 0.4 is an assumed middle value with a wide spread (0.2 to 0.7).
replacement: A sourced within-occupation schooling premium (for example from a wage regression with occupation and employer controls) replacing the assumed share, with the share read per occupation.

whatItFakes: Every lease that exists when the housing records open has its yearly renewal in one of the twelve months after the first review, the month fixed by the hash of the lease id, evenly across the year. No data says when each opening lease was signed.
why: Without it every opening lease renewed on the same review, a year after the opening, so a rent law could reach no tenant in the first year and rents stepped once a year. Leases are signed through the year; the Census table of renters by year moved in (ACS B25038) would give the true spread but is not in the data yet.
replacement: Each opening lease's anniversary drawn from the place's renters by year moved in (ACS B25038), by the same lease-id hash.

whatItFakes: The cap-consumer-loan-rates law applies only to the bank's consumer loan, which sits near 13 percent against a 36 percent ceiling and never reaches it in an ordinary rate year, so no borrower's rate changes and the law moves no dollar. The game has no lender the cap could bind.
why: The owner ruled on Oct 24 that small-dollar lenders are simulated in the background: payday and small-dollar lenders exist where state law allows them, with rates and volumes from sourced data, read by the consumer-loan rate cap and by households that borrow (docs/coordination/OWNER-DECISIONS.md, Oct 24, "Small-dollar lenders"). Until world-small-dollar-lenders builds them, the law is read at every quote and records each household it governed (credit.ts), and its outcome-web link moves lender counts, but no loan is repriced.
replacement: Resolved Oct 29 (world-small-dollar-lenders): the town has a small-dollar lender record where its state's starting law lets payday lending operate (src/core2/modules/credit.ts smallDollarLenderFor, rates from src/core2/data/credit/small-dollar.json), a household the bank does not lend to asks it, and the cap's ceiling binds that quote, so the loan's rate and payment on the journal differ from the uncapped twin's (src/core2/law-wiring-small-dollar-lenders.test.ts).

whatItFakes: Eviction notice, hearing and stay periods are counted in calendar days everywhere. Ten statute reads count other days: business days (Alabama notice 7, Hawaii notice 5, the Northern Marianas notice 3, Utah notice 3 and hearing 3, North Carolina hearing 7), court days (California notice 3, hearing 10), judicial days (West Virginia hearing 5) and days excluding Sundays and legal holidays (the District's summons 30). The table holds the statute's number, so the engine's period is shorter than the statute's for those.
why: The steps table has one number per step and the engine adds days to a date; it has no calendar of business days, court days or legal holidays to count on.
replacement: A day-type per step (calendar, business, court, excluding Sundays and holidays) in the steps table and a counter that skips non-counting days on the place's calendar, read where the engine adds days for the notice, hearing and stay (data/research/world/eviction-statute-reads-2026.json already records each read's dayType).

whatItFakes: When a filled-in household's weight spreads over its group, the households that take it stand for more people while their jobs keep the heads they stood for, so the added people stand for no job and never become counted job seekers.
why: A counted job's heads now stay with its employer through a fill-in (world-counted-weight-release-grows-employer-staff); the jobs engine's counted seekers are read from records, not from the weight a record gains.
replacement: The jobs engine reads each counted record's working-age people beyond its jobs' heads as counted seekers, with the same chooser as everyone else (pool item world-weight-release-jobless-seek-work).

whatItFakes: A filled-in record whose job stood for less than one job, at an employer with no other counted job, becomes one full job: that employer gains the difference (under one head).
why: A full person holds a whole job, and with no other counted job at the employer there is no record to take the difference back from.
replacement: The employer's staffing review reads the full job against its staffing need and sheds or keeps it by its own books, as for any job.

whatItFakes: Puerto Rico place 7237336's counted renter households earn about a third of the ACS income, so half of them pay over 72 percent of income in rent on day one; their living-cost arrears then push 17 households into homelessness (76 per 10,000 against HUD's 6.5), and the housing-calibration case is pinned to that count instead of the HUD bound.
why: Counted incomes in Puerto Rico are read at a third of the sourced figure (pool item world-counted-renter-income-puerto-rico-third); with rent now read from the territory's own counties, the arrears from living costs (#4937) show it as homelessness.
replacement: Correct the counted renters' income to the place's sourced ratio (world-counted-renter-income-puerto-rico-third), then remove the pin so the case meets the HUD bound.

whatItFakes: A worker at an employer with no business books (a town, county or state government, or another public body) gets the yearly move with the place's pay level but no raise for tenure or how they work, so a public employee's pay does not grow within the job as a private worker's does.
why: A business's raises are held to the room its own trading month leaves; a public employer has no trading month, and its pay follows its budget line and the public pay floor (public-pay-floor.ts, the bargaining law). Public step schedules and the budget room they would read are not modeled yet.
replacement: Within-job raises for public workers by the same withinJobRaise rule, held to the room in the government's personnel budget line (the budgets engine) or set by the step schedule a bargaining or pay law records.

whatItFakes: Every job held at the opening counts its tenure from the game's start, so each opening worker's first yearly raise reads the steepest year of the tenure profile (about 2.6 points over the market's move) instead of the year their real tenure would put them in (about 1.0 point at the BLS median of 3.9 years).
why: The opening records no start date for anyone's job (src/core2/deep-past.ts keeps only a supplied start and assigns no median to a missing job history), so tenure within a firm spans a few days at the start; the same gap is why traitWeightJobsValueWorker is sized against real tenure rather than the played world's.
replacement: An opening start date for each job held at the opening, generated from the BLS Employee Tenure tables by age and industry when the world is generated (who exists may be seeded), read by tenureYears for raises and layoffs alike.
resolution: Each job held at the opening carries when it was taken (the work commitment's heldSince): the world's recorded start, else the opening's estimate from the BLS age band's median tenure bounded by adulthood and the employer's founding, the same date the person's work:opening fact and their opening pay read (src/core2/population.ts, openingStartOf). tenureYears reads it for full and counted workers alike, so raises, layoffs and quits read real tenure (pool item people-opening-job-tenure-estimate).

whatItFakes: Three helpers draw a world's offset around a published figure with the same rule (macro-model worldOffset, the budgets module's budgetWorldFactor, world-draw's worldOffsetShare), each with its own floor parameter of the same value.
why: Each source table was drawn in its own PR the same night; folding the macro and budget draws into world-draw would touch two merged readers and their tests in a statistics PR.
replacement: Resolved Oct 28 (wire-office): world-draw.ts's worldOffsetUnit is the one draw; macroWorldOffsets, the regional offsets, budgetWorldFactor, housingWorldOffset and the outcome web's drawnBaseOf multiply it by their own spread row, and the macro, budget, housing and outcome-web floor parameters are deleted for worldDrawOffsetFloorShare.

whatItFakes: A legislative seat whose district has no contested 2024 result on record keeps its real 2026 holder's party in every world: the uncontested seats (safe for their party) and the whole chambers that did not vote in 2024 (Alabama, Louisiana, Maryland, Mississippi, New Jersey and Virginia elect in other years; Nebraska's is nonpartisan; Washington's and the District's results are not in the file). Only seats a world's swing carries across even change hands.
why: The world's swing moves a seat only through its own 2024 vote, and these seats have none on record (MEDSL 2024 state legislative returns, doi:10.7910/DVN/DODOBJ).
replacement: Each such seat's last contested result (2022 or 2023 returns for the chambers that vote in other years, the district's presidential vote where none), read the same way.

whatItFakes: One small-dollar lender record stands for every high-cost lender in a town (storefront payday, installment, vehicle title and online), at the state's one sourced rate, payday or installment by state. It checks every applicant for its own earlier charge-offs, where the CFPB finds only some lenders check a specialty credit reporting firm for earlier payday defaults (white paper, April 2013, page 9). A lender never opens or closes in play: a state that repeals its cap or bans the product gains or loses none. The outcome web's factor on high-cost lenders (the count of storefronts the research moves) stands in for lenders closing by shrinking what the one lender lends a household, not by turning households away, and the cap's ceiling lowers the payment a household weighs, so under the cap a household short of money is as likely or likelier to borrow, where the research finds use falls as lenders leave.
why: The credit engine had no lender beside the town bank. The sourced rates are one per state (CRL's single-payment payday map, NCLC's installment cap), the sourced volume is a national household share, and the Census count of consumer-lending storefronts per state (the web's finance.high-cost-loans base) is not yet read to place one lender per storefront or to mix products. With one lender that never closes, the web's factor can only scale its loans: the price path (the ceiling, read at the quote) and the supply path (the factor, read where the lender sizes the loan) are both live, each from its own record, and neither stands for the other.
replacement: One lender record per storefront, from the place's share of the state's Census consumer-lending establishments (data/research/outcome-web/place-outcome-bases-2024.json, finance.high-cost-loans), each with a product (payday, installment, title) and its own rate, opening and closing as the law in force and the web's count move.

whatItFakes: The town's small-dollar lender pays no costs and draws nothing out: every dollar of interest and fees its borrowers pay stays in its cash and is lent again, so its room to lend grows with each month's interest.
why: The lender is one organization record with cash (smallDollarLenderFor); the credit engine keeps no books for it beyond the loans it writes and the payments it takes, as the town bank kept none before deposits were built. A storefront's rent, wages, loan losses and the owner's profit are not yet sourced.
replacement: The lender's costs (storefront rent, wages, charge-offs) and its owner's draw paid out of its cash each month, sized from the sourced industry margin (the operating costs and pre-tax margin of publicly traded payday lenders' annual reports, or the CFPB's and FDIC's studies of storefront lending costs), so its room to lend is its capital plus what it keeps after costs.

whatItFakes: A household with any open loan, the bank's or the storefront's, asks neither the bank nor the small-dollar lender: the lender copies the bank's one-open-loan rule, so a payday borrower never holds two payday loans at once or a payday loan beside a bank loan.
why: The credit engine checks one set of open loans for both lenders. State payday laws differ on concurrent loans (some allow one at a time with a statewide database check, some two, some set no limit), and that is not yet a sourced row per state.
replacement: Each state's limit on concurrent small-dollar loans as a row in src/core2/data/credit/small-dollar.json (from the state's statute, e.g. NCSL's payday lending statutes table), read where the lender quotes, with the bank's own rule kept for the bank.

whatItFakes: A town whose drawn yearly small-dollar volume could not fund one $100 loan gets no lender record, so its households short of money have no high-cost lender at all, and the consumer-loan cap has nothing to bind there.
why: The lender record is per town, from the town's own households (about 30 households or fewer at the sourced share and volume), and the world keeps no record of the lenders in neighboring places its people could reach.
replacement: Borrowers in a town without a storefront reach the nearest place's lender (a coarse-tier lender for the county or the nearest place with one), quoted under the law in force where the lender operates.

whatItFakes: An eviction's push toward leaving town (movesEvictedPull, 0.35) lands on a counted household as a raised rate of leaving, times exp(0.35), for as long as the eviction leaves it without a home (tenure none, its housing status row naming an eviction case); a full person takes the same push once, on the day of the housing.eviction, added to a pull that keeps it until they decide (moves.ts EVENT_PULLS). A household a foreclosure removed takes no push on either tier, since a foreclosure records no eviction.
why: The counted tier moves by expected rates accrued monthly by group, with no per-household pull carried from month to month; a household without a home is the record the eviction left, so its rate is the one place the push can land (CTO ruling, Nov 1: an evicted counted household stays counted).
replacement: A counted household's own pull carried month to month (the push added once on the day, faded as a full person's), or the push calibrated against the share of evicted households that leave their county (Desmond and Shollenberger 2015).

whatItFakes: A counted household's eviction names its members with a record (person records, and husks: relatives a full person knows) and the rest by its facts, so a watched relative reads it through the director's place reach and the press prints it from its counted subjects; but the full people who list a counted member as family learn of it only as any reader in town does. On main the evicted household was filled in, and its members, as full people, passed the news on at each contact (news.ts) to the relatives fill-in tied them to; counted members pass nothing on, and the eviction names no full relative as a witness.
why: CTO ruling, Nov 1: an evicted counted household stays counted until it comes to matter to the player. Naming the full relatives as witnesses (as births-counted notifyCountedDeaths does for a counted death, the precedent) would make each of them perceive the eviction on the day: the drives engine would answer them, the director would appraise them as named, and neither has been checked to read a relative's eviction as a relative's rather than as the subject's.
replacement: The eviction names as witnesses the full people who know a counted member (the full people who list them as family, and their ties), as notifyCountedDeaths does for a counted death, once drives, trait change and the director read a witness to a relative's eviction by their relation; or counted members pass news on at contact by the news engine's rule.
